dataset.t: Our **twelve customers**, with no labels, plotted by purchases per month and average spend. The goal is to **group them by similarity**.

choose-k.t: K-Means needs the **number of clusters in advance**. Here we choose **K = 3**. We will see later that this choice matters.

initial-centers.t: Start with three **centers** (diamonds), here at (3, 4), (5, 3) and (5, 9.5). They live in the **same space as the data** and are only a first guess.

nearest-center.t: Every customer finds the center **nearest** to it. The thin lines show these choices.

assign-groups.t: Each customer joins the group of its nearest center. The grouping is rough: the customer at **(6.8, 6.8)** joined the wrong clump.

compute-means.t: For each group, find the **mean position** of its members (the crosses). This is where the center would sit if it were in the middle of its points.

move-centers.t: Each center **moves to the mean of its group**. The centers now fit their groups better than the starting guess.

repeat.t: With the centers moved, assign again: the stray customer **switches groups**. Then move the centers once more.

final-clusters.t: Now nothing changes: **three clusters** with centers near (1.68, 2.0), (6.58, 6.12) and (3.67, 8.28). K-Means **alternates assign and move** until the groups are stable.
